summary: Defines a MIME content type that a mail transfer agent or gateway uses to report the result of attempts to deliver a message to one or more recipients. It is meant as a machine-processable replacement for the many ad hoc bounce formats then in use.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3464 defines a standard format for email delivery reports. Mail programs can use it to identify which message and recipient the report concerns and whether delivery succeeded, failed, or is still being attempted.

subtitle: A machine-readable format for reporting email delivery results to senders.

tldr.problem: Mail systems used many notification formats, making it difficult for programs to identify the message, recipient, and reason for a delivery result consistently.
tldr.mechanism: A Delivery Status Notification uses a multipart/report message with a structured message/delivery-status part. That part separates fields about the message from one group of fields for each recipient.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3464 defines the notification format, obsoletes RFC 1894, and has been updated by RFC 4865, RFC 5337, and RFC 6533.

today: RFC 3464 is a Draft Standard published in January 2003 and obsoletes RFC 1894. It has been updated by RFC 4865, RFC 5337, and RFC 6533.

sections.title: What a Delivery Status Notification Reports
sections.content:
A Delivery Status Notification (DSN) reports the result of trying to deliver a message to one or more recipients. It can report failed delivery, delay, success, or a handoff to a mail environment that may not support DSNs. RFC 3464 defines the format; a separate SMTP extension specifies how clients request these notifications.

The format is intended for people and programs. It helps a mail program associate a report with the original message, supports mailing-list maintenance, and can carry addresses or error codes from other mail systems.
sections.plainLanguage: A DSN tells a sender what happened when a mail system tried to deliver a message. The format lets software connect the report to the message and the affected recipient.

sections.title: The Parts of a DSN
sections.content:
A DSN is a multipart/report message with report type delivery-status. It contains a human-readable explanation, a message/delivery-status part, and may include the original message or part of it. One DSN describes one message, but it can report results for several recipients.

The structured part uses mail header-field syntax. Per-message fields appear first, followed by a blank line and one or more per-recipient groups, each separated by a blank line. The field names are case-insensitive, and the body must use 7-bit encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: A DSN has a readable explanation and a structured part that programs can parse. It describes one original message and gives each recipient a separate result.

sections.title: Fields That Apply to the Whole Message
sections.content:
Per-message fields apply to the report as a whole and may appear no more than once. Reporting-MTA is required; it names the mail transfer agent (MTA) that attempted delivery, relaying, or gatewaying. Optional fields can identify the original submission transaction, the gateway that translated a foreign report, the MTA that handed over the message, and its arrival time.

Names and addresses that may use different formats include a type label before the value, such as dns; host.example. This lets a DSN preserve information from systems with different naming conventions.
sections.plainLanguage: The first group identifies the mail system reporting the result and may add details about the original message. Type labels show which format to use when reading an address or system name.

sections.title: Fields for Each Recipient
sections.content:
Each recipient group must include Final-Recipient, Action, and Status. The final-recipient value is the address held by the reporting MTA and may differ from the address the sender originally supplied. Optional fields can preserve that original address, a transport-specific diagnostic, the remote MTA, and dates.

Action describes the result: failed, delayed, delivered, relayed, or expanded. The transport-independent Status code begins with 2 for success, 4 for a persistent temporary failure, or 5 for a permanent failure. A delivered action means the message reached the address, not that anyone read it.
sections.plainLanguage: Each recipient gets a result describing whether delivery failed, is continuing, or reached an address. A separate status code gives a general class of result, while an optional diagnostic can preserve the mail system's own detail.

sections.title: Adding Types and Extension Fields
sections.content:
IANA maintains registries for address types, diagnostic types, and MTA-name types. Names beginning with X- are reserved for experimental use and are not registered. A type label tells software how to interpret the value that follows it.

Later specifications may define additional per-message or per-recipient fields. New standard field names must be registered with IANA and published in an RFC; names beginning with X- remain experimental. Extension fields can preserve details from foreign systems or help an MTA administrator investigate a problem.
sections.plainLanguage: Type registries tell programs how to interpret different address and diagnostic formats. New standard fields need a published definition, while names starting with X- are for experiments.

sections.title: Implementation and Mailing-List Use
sections.content:
A minimal implementation generates the reporting MTA and, for each recipient, the final recipient, action, and status. An MTA must not report an original recipient address unless the mail transport supplied it. Mailing-list software can examine DSNs and remove subscribers whose delivery repeatedly fails, but the RFC advises against removing an address after one failure or a delayed report.

Over SMTP, a DSN must use the null return address MAIL FROM:<> to prevent notification loops. A DSN can be forged like ordinary email, and an apparently failed delivery does not prove that the recipient received nothing: duplicate delivery attempts can produce both a successful delivery and a failure report.
sections.plainLanguage: Mailing lists can use repeated failures to identify addresses that may no longer work. They should not act on a single report, because reports can be forged or delivery attempts can have mixed results.

viz.caption: THE FIVE ACTION VALUES FOR A RECIPIENT

items.label: Delayed
items.desc: The reporting MTA will continue trying.

items.label: Delivered
items.desc: Reached the address; this does not mean it was read.

items.label: Relayed
items.desc: Passed into an environment that does not report delivery.

items.label: Expanded
items.desc: Delivered to an address and forwarded to multiple addresses.
